passages.t: ‘Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven’, and the cost of silence
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “Of David. A Maskil” (verse 1). Then two blessings. “Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered” (verse 1). “Blessed is the man whose iniquity the LORD does not count against him, in whose spirit there is no deceit” (verse 2).

Then he tells what happened when he hid his sin. “When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long” (verse 3). “For day and night Your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was drained as in the summer heat” (verse 4).

And what happened when he stopped hiding. “Then I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the LORD,’ and You forgave the guilt of my sin” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Maskil is a heading word whose meaning is uncertain. It may mean a skilful song or a song that teaches. This is the first psalm to carry it.

Verses 1 and 2 use three words for wrong. ‘Transgressions’ are acts of rebellion, crossing a line on purpose. ‘Sins’ are missing the mark. ‘Iniquity’ is crookedness, a twist in the heart. Then three words for God's answer: forgiven (lifted off), covered, not counted. Every kind of wrong has a remedy.

Two words come back in verse 5. ‘Covered’ in verse 1 is the same Hebrew word as ‘hide’ in verse 5. While he covered his sin, it stayed. When he stopped covering it, God covered it. And ‘forgiven’ in verse 1 is the same word as ‘forgave’ in verse 5.

‘Summer heat’ would hit home in Israel, where months pass with no rain at all and the land dries out. Hidden guilt, he says, dried him up like that.

Psalm 32 is one of the church's seven penitential psalms, prayers of sorrow for sin (see the note on Psalm 6). Unlike Psalm 6, it does confess sin, and it says what confession did.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verses 1 and 2 in his letter to the Romans. He uses them to show that God puts people right with himself as a gift, not as wages. “David speaks likewise of the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works: ‘Blessed are they whose lawless acts are forgiven, whose sins are covered.’” (Romans 4:6-7).

Proverbs agrees with verse 3: “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). And John writes, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).
passages.hard:
Verses 3 and 4 tie hidden sin to a body wasting away. Does that mean illness is a sign of hidden sin?

No. The psalm describes what one man's hidden guilt did to him. It does not say that every illness has a sin behind it, and the Bible says plainly elsewhere that it does not (John 9:2-3; the book of Job). Many people are ill who have hidden nothing.

What the psalm does say is true to life. Guilt kept secret can weigh on body and mind. If you are carrying something you have never told anyone, the psalm's answer is to bring it into the light, to God first, and often to a trusted person too (James 5:16). Psalm 51 gives words for that.
passages.asks:
Is there something you are keeping silent about? The psalm does not shame you. It tells you what silence costs, and what confession gives.

Notice how quickly God forgives in verse 5. ‘I said, I will confess’, and the next words are ‘You forgave’. Forgiveness is not something you have to earn by feeling bad for long enough.

passages.t: ‘You are my hiding place’, and the horse and the mule
passages.happening:
Now he speaks to others. “Therefore let all the godly pray to You while You may be found. Surely when great waters rise, they will not come near” (verse 6).

“You are my hiding place. You protect me from trouble; You surround me with songs of deliverance” (verse 7).

Then a new voice speaks, it seems God's own. “I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go; I will give you counsel and watch over you” (verse 8). “Do not be like the horse or mule, which have no understanding; they must be controlled with bit and bridle to make them come to you” (verse 9).

The psalm ends in joy. “loving devotion surrounds him who trusts in the LORD” (verse 10). “Be glad in the LORD and rejoice, O righteous ones” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
‘Great waters’ stood for danger and chaos. The forgiven person has a place to hide when the flood rises.

Look at the change. Before, he hid his sin from God. Now he hides in God. The one he was running from has become his shelter.

A horse or a mule has to be steered with a metal bit in its mouth and a bridle, pulled this way and that, because it will not come of its own will. God wants people who come because they understand, not because they are dragged.

‘Surrounds’ in verse 10 echoes verse 7. God surrounds him with songs, and with hesed, his faithful love.
passages.later:
Isaiah calls people to come while there is time: “Seek the LORD while He may be found” (Isaiah 55:6). Jesus told of a son who came home after wasting everything and said, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you” (Luke 15:21). The father ran to meet him.

Paul tells the difference between two kinds of sorrow: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).
passages.hard:
‘While You may be found’ (verse 6). Is there a time when it is too late to come to God?

The psalm's point is not to make people afraid that the door has shut. It is the urgency of love: do not wait until the waters rise. Everywhere else the Bible shows God's mercy reaching people others had given up on. Anyone who wants to come back to God is, by that very wish, being called.
passages.asks:
Verse 9 asks how you are led. Do you wait for life to pull you by the bit before you turn, or do you come when God calls?

Try praying verse 7 slowly: ‘You are my hiding place.’ Then name what you are hiding from, and let him be the place you hide.
